URL: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/18/kemi-badenoch-andy-burnham-consensus-politics-pmqs
The Guardian (John Crace), 18 Nov 2026 17:35 GMT

The Tory leader is hardwired for conflict. It was futile for the PM to demand an end to her patronising tone

Well, that didn’t take long. When Andy Burnham first arrived in No 10, he said he was determined to do things differently. He wanted a new, consensual politics where he would work with other parties to put the country back together. Safe to say, that dream is already dead in the water. At least when it comes to his exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions.

Andy might go through the motions of promising Ed Davey and various backbenchers a veneer of cross-party support that may or may not become reality – even Andy doesn’t have a clue which is which – but when it comes to Kemi, it’s now just a bloodless slanging match. Bloodless because there’s nothing really at stake. It’s all just a performance. Kemi has yet to land a blow on Burnham, so both leaders are merely playing to a gallery of their own backbenchers.

In fairness, it’s probably easiest this way. Even if Andy were to say: “You know what, Kemi? I think you’re right. Let’s try doing it your way,” Kemi would still find a way to say that would be the wrong thing to do. She is hardwired for conflict. And if there’s no one on hand for her to disagree with, she will happily round on herself. She is lost without someone to fight.

All of which leaves Andy and Kemi on cruise control, with PMQs a jeopardy-free zone. There were times when Keir Starmer was prime minister it felt as if he might fall apart on a Wednesday lunchtime. Not least when facing questions over his suicidal decision to appoint Peter Mandelson as ambassador to Washington. But Andy has no apparent weak spots. Certainly none that Kemi has so far identified. And she doesn’t seem particularly interested in doing much work to find them. So she goes into each session with no real idea of what she is hoping to achieve. Other than to have an argument that everyone will soon forget.

All of which suits Burnham just fine. He can tick off 12pm on Wednesday as a comparatively stress-free zone. So much so that he is even quite happy making fun of himself. In his traditional opening line of: “This morning I have had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others” he managed to add in an “according to ChatGPT”. A nod to one of his advisers being caught on a train last weekend using AI while drafting a speech.

Then we got the phoney war. Kemi chose to attack on welfare and Neets. It was what she had on her mind, so she might as well. When was the welfare bill going to come down, she asked. And why would everything the government did take at least 10 years? If Kemi had thought for a nanosecond, she could have answered the second question herself. It was taking that long because the Tories had done nothing about it for 14 years. Er … and if it was simple to fix, governments would have done it long ago.

View image in fullscreenKemi told Andy he wanted welfare vibes, not welfare cuts – this was Kemi as ‘Disgusted of Saffron Walden’. Photograph: House of Commons/PABurnham initially chose to try to give Kemi a straight answer. The reason the welfare bill wouldn’t come down was because of the way the accounts were balanced. Some young people would get less in benefits but receive more in help to get them back to work. Then Andy looked up and saw that Kemi hadn’t been paying attention. He might as well have been talking to the hand. At which moment he rather gave up and resorted to the lowest common denominator: point-scoring. Kemi and her sidekick the shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, were just too dumb to understand anything. They wouldn’t be happy until they saw someone really suffer by having their benefits removed. Blood lust.

Now PMQs deteriorated into a charade. Kemi immediately countered by saying she understood everything perfectly and it was the prime minister who understood nothing. He just wanted welfare vibes, not welfare cuts. This was Kemi as “Disgusted of Saffron Walden”. Disgusted for the sake of being disgusted. For Andy, it was open warfare. Whatever else the Milburn review might be, it’s not just vibes. It was time for the Tories to show some humility. Kemi was guilty of choosing her facts selectively. Something he would naturally never do. Except he would. It may be a pointless fight, but it might as well be a dirty one.

Read moreThere was still time for Kemi to misunderstand the deal with the EU: she assumed what had been agreed was 100,000 foreigners coming to the UK and no Brits going to Europe. By now, Burnham had had enough. Enough of the patronising tone, he said. He might as well have asked for time to stop. Patronising is what Kemi does. It’s almost a sign of endearment. Her way of expressing affection.

A few Tories liked to imagine that this was a major misstep on Burnham’s part. That to say something that has been blindingly obvious for a couple of years now was in some way a sign of weakness. That Kemi had got to him. In which case how many other truths are there that cannot be mentioned? The real point was that this was yet another PMQs where Burnham had come across as the more human, more likable politician. There’s a reason Labour is a long way clear in the opinion polls. Most people think the party is doing a decent job.

One cabinet minister missing from this week’s PMQs was the home secretary. Shabana Mahmood was at a police chiefs’ conference to give a speech on “two-tier policing”. Shabana is the government’s fall guy who willingly gets sent out to defend anything that might be seen as Reform adjacent. She wasn’t saying there was two-tier policing, but there again, she wasn’t saying there wasn’t. Maybe we could settle on police that target everyone. That’s something we could all get behind.
